title: Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following

paper.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following
paper.abstract:
Abstract Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfaction but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying request, creating an evaluation blind spot.
We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content.
Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
To address this reward hacking, we introduce CaLIF , a lightweight method that augments verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response quality. CaLIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward model.
Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning modes, CaLIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining response quality near or above pre-RL levels.
It also outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons across three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Instruction following is central to the practical use of large language models (LLMs), enabling them to translate user intent into desired outputs ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Chung et al., 2024 ) . In real-world applications, a user input typically comprises a request , which specifies the task to be performed, and one or more constraints , which define the conditions the response must satisfy ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Successful instruction following therefore requires both high Response Quality by providing a substantive answer to the request and high Constraint Satisfaction by adhering to the stated constraints. However, achieving both objectives consistently remains challenging even for highly capable models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Evaluating instruction following for open-ended user inputs heavily relies on human assessment or LLM judgments, which can be costly, subjective, and sensitive to the choice of evaluator ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Thakur et al., 2025 ) . Verifiable instruction-following (VIF) benchmarks ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ) address these evaluation challenges by focusing on requirements that can be checked programmatically. IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) , for example, appends output constraints to a request and measures Constraint Satisfaction using programmatic verifiers, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation without relying on LLM judges. Consequently, VIF benchmarks are widely used to assess the capability for instruction following. For example, Artificial Analysis, one of the most widely used AI evaluation platforms, assesses instruction following using only IFBench’s Constraint Satisfaction scores ( Artificial Analysis, 2026 ) . However, these scores do not capture how well a response answers the request ( i.e. , Response Quality ): verifiers check only whether the constraint is met, and a response that ignores the request scores just as well as one that answers it fully. Indeed, we observe responses that receive full verifier credit for satisfying constraints while failing to adequately answer requests they handle well without those constraints (Figure 2 ). Moreover, using three strong LLM judges, we find that current frontier models with higher Constraint Satisfaction tend to have lower Response Quality (Figure 1(a) ). These findings expose an evaluation blind spot in VIF benchmarks: high Constraint Satisfaction can be mistaken for strong instruction-following ability even when responses fail to answer the request. Beyond evaluation, programmatic verification can be naturally integrated with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), a widely used approach for LLM post-training ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025a ) . IF-RLVR ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) applies this approach to instruction following using verifier-based rewards for Constraint Satisfaction , yielding substantial gains on VIF benchmarks. However, in the publicly released OLMo 3 family ( Olmo et al., 2025 ) , whose RL training includes VIF task alongside other tasks, we observe higher Constraint Satisfaction but lower Response Quality in RLVR checkpoints than in their DPO counterparts (Figure 3 ). This divergence raises concerns about reward hacking ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Baker et al., 2025 ) , as the verifier reward can reinforce the same response failures that fall into the evaluation blind spot described above. Contribution. In this work, we first diagnose reward hacking in VIF through the lens of Bayes’ rule, and find that the IF-RLVR reward omits the response likelihood under the request alone. Naively adding this term back, however, induces a different failure mode: the policy produces responses that inflate likelihood without genuinely improving response quality, e.g. , repetitions. To mitigate this failure mode, we introduce Ca librated L ikelihood for I nstruction F ollowing ( CaLIF ), which effectively co-optimizes response quality during IF-RLVR by calibrating the verifier reward using a prompt-specific likelihood region. The key intuition is to define the desired behavior of the trained policy relative to two reference responses from the pre-RL policy: the response it produces under the request with constraints, and the one without them. The former’s likelihood provides a baseline for preserving or improving response quality, while the latter’s likelihood provides a reference for preventing likelihood inflation, since increases beyond the unconstrained reference need not reflect better answers. These likelihoods define the region’s lower and upper bounds, respectively. We retain the verifier reward below the lower bound, add a fixed bonus within the region when the verifier reward is positive, and set the total reward to zero above the upper bound. In practice, CaLIF adds little overhead: it reuses the reference policy already maintained for KL regularization, computes both bounds offline, and requires at most one extra teacher-forced forward pass per rollout. Constraint Satisfaction evaluates whether responses satisfy the constraints using programmatic verifiers; Response Quality evaluates how well they answer the request using three LLM judges: GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, whose scores are averaged. Pink arrows show the drop in Response Quality from answering the request alone to answering the request with added constraints. Across five model configurations spanning 1.7B to 8B parameters and including both thinking and non-thinking modes, CaLIF improves Constraint Satisfaction on IFBench while keeping Response Quality near or above base-policy levels. On average across these configurations, IF-RLVR increases Constraint Satisfaction (0–100 scale) from 26.98 to 44.93 but reduces Response Quality (1–10 scale) from 4.51 to 2.96, while CaLIF improves both metrics to 34.64 and 4.59, respectively. Focusing on prompts where the base policy fails constraint verification but the trained policy passes, we find an average decline in Response Quality of 0.28 points under CaLIF , compared with 2.05 under IF-RLVR, which indicates that CaLIF learns to satisfy constraints with substantially less degradation in its answers to the request. Importantly, these gains generalize to three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, where CaLIF outperforms baselines in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons, versus only 14 of 45 for IF-RLVR. These results demonstrate that CaLIF ’s reference-calibrated reward provides an effective signal for mitigating reward hacking in IF-RLVR without any additional models or explicit supervision. CaLIF thus brings the scalability of verifiable rewards to the full objective of instruction following: satisfying constraints while adequately answering the request. The model achieves a high Response Quality score of 9.33 when given the request alone, but its constrained response includes exactly five numbers as required while scoring only 2.00 in Response Quality .

sections.heading: 2.1 Instruction-Following Evaluation
sections.text: Instruction following has been extensively studied as a core capability of LLMs. MT-Bench ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) and AlpacaEval ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) use LLM judges to rate response quality or compare responses, providing a scalable alternative to human evaluation. Further work extends LLM-based evaluation to individual requirements and their combinations, using task-specific rubrics for finer-grained assessment ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks assess satisfaction of explicit constraints through programmatic checks rather than LLM judgments, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation ( He et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Jaroslawicz et al., 2025 ; Liquid AI, 2026 ) . As an example, IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) covers constraints on response length, keyword inclusion, and output format, while IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) extends this approach to a broader range of output constraints.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reward Hacking in RLVR
sections.text: Reward hacking occurs when optimizing a proxy reward leads to behavior that diverges from the intended objective ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Pan et al., 2022 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ) . In RLVR, models can exploit flaws or misspecifications in verification procedures to obtain higher rewards without improving performance on the intended task ( Baker et al., 2025 ; MacDiarmid et al., 2025 ; Helff et al., 2026 ) , with related concerns reported in IF-RLVR ( Guo et al., 2025b ; Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) . To mitigate this behavior, prior work supplements verifiable rewards with explicit feedback on instruction fulfillment, using learned preference reward models ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) or LLM-based intent checks ( Guo et al., 2025b ) . These approaches, however, require maintaining and querying an additional reward model or LLM judge during training, introducing memory and inference overhead.

sections.heading: 3 The Evaluation Blind Spot in Verifiable Instruction Following
sections.text: Instruction-following benchmarks assess how well a model’s response y y fulfills the user’s request and requirements. Because evaluating open-ended responses relies on costly human assessment or potentially biased LLM judgments ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) , verifiable instruction-following (VIF) benchmarks such as IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) focus on programmatically verifiable requirements. Specifically, these benchmarks append output constraints c c to a request x x and use programmatic verifiers to check whether y y satisfies c c , enabling scalable, reproducible evaluation without relying on LLM judges. Successful instruction following requires y y to satisfy c c while providing a substantive answer to x x , but standard VIF evaluation focuses primarily on constraint compliance. In practice, Artificial Analysis and several frontier model technical reports use only IFBench’s constraint compliance scores to assess models’ instruction-following performance ( Artificial Analysis, 2026 ) . To examine how frontier models balance these requirements, we evaluate both Constraint Satisfaction , which measures whether y y satisfies c c , and Response Quality , which measures how well y y answers x x . We compute the former as IFBench’s prompt-level loose accuracy and the latter as the mean 1–10 prompt–completion rating from strong LLM judges (see Appendix A for details). Figure 1(a) shows substantial variation across models, with higher Constraint Satisfaction tending to coincide with lower Response Quality . To assess whether this relationship simply reflects differences in models’ ability to answer x x , we compare each model’s responses under x x and ( x , c ) (x,c) . Figure 1(b) shows that all models in this comparison achieve high Response Quality under x x alone, but appending c c degrades Response Quality , with the largest declines among models with the highest Constraint Satisfaction . Figure 2 illustrates this degradation in a model that provides a substantive explanation under x x alone but returns only “No. 0 1 2 3 4,” under ( x , c ) (x,c) . Standard VIF evaluation counts this response as successful solely because it satisfies c c , exposing an evaluation blind spot . Figure 3: Comparison of DPO and RLVR checkpoints in the OLMo 3 family on IFBench. Log-likelihood is computed under the corresponding DPO checkpoint, conditioned on the request alone. IF-RLVR ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) extends this verifier-based criterion from evaluation to training, applying RLVR to instruction following with rewards derived from programmatic verification of the appended constraints. However, models trained with RL for instruction following ( NVIDIA, 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) tend to show high Constraint Satisfaction but low Response Quality , as noted above. Furthermore, in all three matched OLMo 3 ( Olmo et al., 2025 ) DPO–RLVR pairs, the RLVR checkpoint achieves higher Constraint Satisfaction but lower Response Quality (Figure 3 ). These observations are consistent with reward hacking under IF-RLVR, where models improve verifier rewards at the expense of response quality ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Pan et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We now evaluate whether CaLIF can mitigate the reward-hacking failure identified above through matched comparisons with IF-RLVR across model scales, thinking modes, and model families.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: For the training dataset, we use the multi-constraint IF-RLVR data released with IFBench, 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/IF_multi_constraints_upto5 comprising 95,373 prompts constructed by augmenting instructions from the Tülu 3 SFT mixture ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) with one to five verifiable constraints from IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) and IFTrain ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) . We train Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B in both thinking and non-thinking modes ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and Tülu 3 8B DPO ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) in verl . 2 2 2 https://github.com/verl-project/verl We use matched training settings for CaLIF and IF-RLVR, with a rollout temperature of 1.0 1.0 and a KL loss coefficient β = 0.001 \beta=0.001 , and set likelihood reward coefficient α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 for CaLIF . For offline reference generation, responses are sampled with a temperature of 1.0 1.0 . In thinking mode, responses include reasoning traces, but only final answers are scored under the reference policy in non-thinking mode. For evaluation, we follow the providers’ recommended settings and report the mean and standard deviation over three runs. Unless otherwise specified, we use GPT-5.6 Sol to rate Response Quality on a 1–10 scale. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: CaLIF Mitigates Reward Hacking in IF-RLVR.
sections.text: Figure 5 compares CaLIF with IF-RLVR on IFBench across five model configurations. IF-RLVR increases Constraint Satisfaction at the expense of Response Quality in every configuration, with average quality falling from 4.51 to 2.96. By contrast, CaLIF raises average Constraint Satisfaction from 26.98 to 34.64 (+7.66 points) while preserving Response Quality at an average of 4.59. Pairwise evaluation further supports this quality advantage, with CaLIF achieving an overall adjusted win rate of 78.10% against IF-RLVR (see Appendix D.1 ). As shown in Figure 6 , reference log-likelihood under the request alone follows a similar pattern, decreasing under IF-RLVR but remaining near base-policy levels under CaLIF . Together, these results show that CaLIF ’s reference-calibrated reward mitigates reward hacking, retaining gains in Constraint Satisfaction without the quality degradation observed under IF-RLVR. sections.heading: CaLIF Generalizes Beyond Verifiable Constraints.
sections.text: To assess generalization to broader instruction-following requirements, we evaluate on three rubric-based benchmarks whose criteria cover both Constraint Satisfaction and Response Quality : AdvancedIF ( He et al., 2026 ) , FollowBench ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) , and ComplexBench ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . As shown in Table 1 , CaLIF improves over the base policies in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons, compared with only 14 for IF-RLVR. CaLIF also outperforms IF-RLVR in 41 of 45 comparisons, with all four exceptions confined to Format , the dimension most closely aligned with the training constraints. These results demonstrate that CaLIF generalizes beyond verifiable constraints to broader instruction following.

sections.heading: Harder Constraints Amplify Reward Hacking.
sections.text: Figure 7 shows that reward hacking under IF-RLVR is most severe for harder constraint types. On word-level constraints, where base policies struggle most, IF-RLVR achieves its largest gains in Constraint Satisfaction but also the largest decline in Response Quality . This decline is accompanied by a marked reduction in response length, suggesting that the policy satisfies c c while omitting substantive content needed to answer x x . By contrast, CaLIF improves constraint satisfaction across constraint types while maintaining response quality near or above base-policy levels, without the response shortening observed under IF-RLVR.

We consider two sources of supervision: the base policy itself ( Self-judge ) and a more capable model, Qwen3-30B-A3B ( Stronger judge ). Following Pyatkin et al. Another advantage of CaLIF is that it requires neither a separate judge model nor judge-score generation. By contrast, CaLIF reuses the existing reference policy, requiring at most one additional teacher-forced forward pass per rollout. sections.heading: 6.1 Direct Likelihood Rewards Encourage Likelihood inflation
sections.text: Our analysis in Section 4 identifies response likelihood under the request alone as a term omitted by IF-RLVR’s verifier reward. To test whether directly rewarding this term preserves Response Quality , we exponentiate the average token log-likelihood to obtain a positive reward bounded by the same α \alpha used in CaLIF . The bonus is applied only when a response receives a positive verifier reward: r direct ( x , c , y ) = r ver ( c , y ) + α exp ( ℓ π ref ( y ; x ) ) [ r ver ( c , y ) > 0 ] . r_{\mathrm{direct}}(x,c,y)=r_{\mathrm{ver}}(c,y)+\alpha\exp\!\left(\ell_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y;x)\right)\mathbf{1}\!\left[r_{\mathrm{ver}}(c,y)>0\right]. However, we find that training with this reward introduces another shortcut (i.e., likelihood inflation ). Relative to the base policy, average reference log-likelihood rises from − 1.50 -1.50 to − 0.68 -0.68 , while Response Quality falls from 3.98 3.98 to 1.91 1.91 (Table 4 ). This deterioration is accompanied by longer, repetitive responses: the average response length increases from 485 to 1,677 tokens, and the fraction of unique token 2-grams is 0.177 0.177 , compared with 0.713 0.713 for the base policy and 0.698 0.698 for CaLIF . The direct reward favors these highly predictable continuations even when they provide less substantive answers to the request, thereby creating another risk to increase reward without improving response quality. We present a qualitative example of likelihood inflation in Appendix D.3 .

sections.heading: 6.2 Both Likelihood Bounds Are Necessary
sections.text: Table 4 shows that the lower and upper likelihood bounds address distinct failure modes. Without the lower bound, low-likelihood responses remain eligible for the bonus: Constraint Satisfaction rises to 43.00 43.00 , but Response Quality falls to 2.16 2.16 . Without the upper bound, responses above the desired region remain eligible for the bonus, leaving the reward vulnerable to likelihood inflation; Response Quality falls to 3.51 3.51 despite increased reference log-likelihood. Among these variants, only the full region improves both dimensions over the base policy. The lower bound discourages deterioration relative to the pre-RL baseline, while the upper bound limits exploitation of the likelihood signal.

We use the inward endpoints to construct a narrower likelihood region and the outward endpoints to construct a wider one. We examine whether stronger KL regularization alone can preserve Response Quality while retaining the gains in Constraint Satisfaction achieved by CaLIF . For CaLIF , we vary α ∈ { 0.001 , 0.01 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.5 , 1.0 } \alpha\in\{\allowbreak 0.001,0.01,\allowbreak 0.1,\allowbreak 0.2,\allowbreak 0.5,\allowbreak 1.0\} while fixing β = 0.001 \beta=0.001 . For IF-RLVR, we vary β ∈ { 0 , 0.001 , 0.002 , 0.005 , 0.01 , 0.02 , 0.05 } \beta\in\{0,\allowbreak 0.001,\allowbreak 0.002,\allowbreak 0.005,\allowbreak 0.01,\allowbreak 0.02,\allowbreak 0.05\} . Across all tested α \alpha values, CaLIF improves Constraint Satisfaction while preserving base-policy Response Quality . Increasing β \beta in IF-RLVR also mitigates quality degradation, but recovering base-policy Response Quality leaves little improvement in Constraint Satisfaction . At β = 0.05 \beta=0.05 , Response Quality matches the base policy at 3.98, while Constraint Satisfaction increases only from 22.22 to 23.00. By contrast, CaLIF at α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 achieves 28.78 in Constraint Satisfaction and 4.01 in Response Quality . These results show that CaLIF retains larger gains in Constraint Satisfaction at comparable Response Quality than IF-RLVR achieves through KL coefficient tuning alone. Moreover, CaLIF remains effective even without explicit KL regularization ( β = 0 \beta=0 ; see Appendix D.2 ).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We identify an evaluation blind spot in verifiable instruction following and document reward hacking in publicly released models. Across five model configurations, CaLIF improves constraint satisfaction while preserving response quality through a reference-calibrated likelihood region, with gains beyond the training verifiers. Our results show that calibrating rather than maximizing reference likelihoods can mitigate reward hacking without additional models or explicit quality supervision.

sections.heading: Training data.
sections.text: We use the multi-constraint IF-RLVR training data released by IFBench. The dataset contains 95,373 prompts constructed by augmenting instructions from the Tülu-3 SFT mixture with one to five automatically verifiable constraints sampled from IFEval and IFTrain.

sections.heading: Models and Training.
sections.text: We use Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B in non-thinking and thinking modes ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and the Tülu 3 8B DPO model ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) . We train all models for four epochs (three for Qwen3-4B in thinking mode due to computational cost) with GRPO in verl on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, using 8 rollouts per prompt, temperature 1.0 1.0 , a global batch size of 1,024 1{,}024 , and a KL loss coefficient of 0.001 0.001 . The maximum response length and learning rate are 2,048 2{,}048 tokens and 5 × 10 − 7 5\times 10^{-7} in non-thinking mode, and 8,192 8{,}192 tokens and 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} in thinking mode.

sections.heading: CaLIF Configuration.
sections.text: We sample anchor responses at the rollout temperature. For thinking models, anchor responses and rollouts include full reasoning traces, but we compute log-likelihoods under π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} in non-thinking mode over final-answer tokens only. We set α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 in all main experiments; Section 6 ablates the two anchors and examines sensitivity to anchor sampling and α \alpha .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We sample with temperature 0.6 0.6 , top- p p 0.95 0.95 , and top- k k 20 20 in thinking mode, and temperature 0.7 0.7 , top- p p 0.8 0.8 , and top- k k 20 20 in non-thinking mode, following official recommendations. We set maximum response lengths of 16,384 16{,}384 and 2,048 2{,}048 tokens for thinking and non-thinking models, respectively. To account for stochasticity, we repeat each evaluation three times and report the mean and standard deviation. Unless otherwise specified, we use GPT-5.6 Sol to rate Response Quality .

sections.heading: AdvancedIF.
sections.text: AdvancedIF ( He et al., 2026 ) evaluates instruction following using expert-written rubrics across three categories: ComplexIF (CIF), Carried Context (CC), and System Steerability (SS). In our experiments, we evaluate only CIF, which focuses on single-turn requests with multiple requirements. We report Overall Pass Rate , the percentage of responses satisfying all rubric criteria, and Micro Rubric Pass Rate , the percentage of satisfied criteria pooled across responses.

sections.heading: FollowBench.
sections.text: FollowBench ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) covers Content, Situation, Style, Format, and Example constraints, along with their combinations (Mixed), across five difficulty levels that progressively add constraints. We report Hard Satisfaction Rate (HSR), the percentage of responses satisfying all constraints; Soft Satisfaction Rate (SSR), the average fraction of constraints satisfied; and Consistent Satisfaction Levels (CSL), the average number of consecutive levels fully satisfied.

sections.heading: ComplexBench.
sections.text: ComplexBench ( Wen et al., 2024 ) evaluates instructions combining constraints through conjunctions, conditional branches, and sequential dependencies. We report scoring-question accuracy for Lexical , Semantic , Utility , and Format constraints, covering word usage, semantic requirements, answer usefulness and factuality, and output format and length, respectively.

sections.heading: D.1 Pairwise Response Quality Evaluation
sections.text: To complement the pointwise Response Quality evaluation, we conduct a pairwise comparison of responses from CaLIF and IF-RLVR using GPT-5.6 Sol as the judge. Following the order-swapping protocol of MT-Bench ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) , we evaluate each pair in both presentation orders. A win or loss is recorded only when both judgments favor the same method; ties in either order and disagreements between orders are counted as ties. We report wins ( W W ), ties ( T T ), and losses ( L L ) from CaLIF ’s perspective and compute the adjusted win rate as ( W + 0.5 ​ T ) / ( W + T + L ) (W+0.5T)/(W+T+L) . Table 5 shows that CaLIF achieves an overall adjusted win rate of 78.10%. These results corroborate the Response Quality advantage of CaLIF over IF-RLVR observed in the pointwise evaluation. sections.heading: D.2 CaLIF without KL Regularization
sections.text: To evaluate whether CaLIF can mitigate reward hacking without KL regularization, we set β = 0 \beta=0 while keeping all other training settings unchanged. Figure 9 compares this variant with default CaLIF and IF-RLVR, both using β = 0.001 \beta=0.001 . With β = 0 \beta=0 , CaLIF still improves Constraint Satisfaction over the base policy while largely preserving Response Quality . These results demonstrate that its reference-calibrated reward can mitigate reward hacking without an explicit KL penalty. Removing the KL penalty eliminates the reference forward pass conditioned on ( x , c ) (x,c) , leaving only the pass conditioned on x x for reward computation. Excluding offline bound construction, CaLIF requires no more reference forward passes per rollout than standard KL-regularized IF-RLVR.

Affiliation: Affiliation: Yonsei University Abstract Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfaction but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying request, creating an evaluation blind spot. We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content. Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To address this reward hacking, we introduce CaLIF , a lightweight method that augments verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response quality. CaLIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward model. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning modes, CaLIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining response quality near or above pre-RL levels. It also outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons across three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers. 1 Introduction Instruction following is central to the practical use of large language models (LLMs), enabling them to translate user intent into desired outputs ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Chung et al., 2024 ) . In real-world applications, a user input typically comprises a request , which specifies the task to be performed, and one or more constraints , which define the conditions the response must satisfy ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Successful instruction following therefore requires both high Response Quality by providing a substantive answer to the request and high Constraint Satisfaction by adhering to the stated constraints. However, achieving both objectives consistently remains challenging even for highly capable models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Evaluating instruction following for open-ended user inputs heavily relies on human assessment or LLM judgments, which can be costly, subjective, and sensitive to the choice of evaluator ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Thakur et al., 2025 ) . Verifiable instruction-following (VIF) benchmarks ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ) address these evaluation challenges by focusing on requirements that can be checked programmatically. IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) , for example, appends output constraints to a request and measures Constraint Satisfaction using programmatic verifiers, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation without relying on LLM judges. Consequently, VIF benchmarks are widely used to assess the capability for instruction following. For example, Artificial Analysis, one of the most widely used AI evaluation platforms, assesses instruction following using only IFBench’s Constraint Satisfaction scores ( Artificial Analysis, 2026 ) . However, these scores do not capture how well a response answers the request ( i.e. , Response Quality ): verifiers check only whether the constraint is met, and a response that ignores the request scores just as well as one that answers it fully. Indeed, we observe responses that receive full verifier credit for satisfying constraints while failing to adequately answer requests they handle well without those constraints (Figure 2 ). Moreover, using three strong LLM judges, we find that current frontier models with higher Constraint Satisfaction tend to have lower Response Quality (Figure 1(a) ). These findings expose an evaluation blind spot in VIF benchmarks: high Constraint Satisfaction can be mistaken for strong instruction-following ability even when responses fail to answer the request. Beyond evaluation, programmatic verification can be naturally integrated with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), a widely used approach for LLM post-training ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025a ) . IF-RLVR ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) applies this approach to instruction following using verifier-based rewards for Constraint Satisfaction , yielding substantial gains on VIF benchmarks. However, in the publicly released OLMo 3 family ( Olmo et al., 2025 ) , whose RL training includes VIF task alongside other tasks, we observe higher Constraint Satisfaction but lower Response Quality in RLVR checkpoints than in their DPO counterparts (Figure 3 ). This divergence raises concerns about reward hacking ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Baker et al., 2025 ) , as the verifier reward can reinforce the same response failures that fall into the evaluation blind spot described above. Contribution. In this work, we first diagnose reward hacking in VIF through the lens of Bayes’ rule, and find that the IF-RLVR reward omits the response likelihood under the request alone. Naively adding this term back, however, induces a different failure mode: the policy produces responses that inflate likelihood without genuinely improving response quality, e.g. , repetitions. To mitigate this failure mode, we introduce Ca librated L ikelihood for I nstruction F ollowing ( CaLIF ), which effectively co-optimizes response quality during IF-RLVR by calibrating the verifier reward using a prompt-specific likelihood region. The key intuition is to define the desired behavior of the trained policy relative to two reference responses from the pre-RL policy: the response it produces under the request with constraints, and the one without them. The former’s likelihood provides a baseline for preserving or improving response quality, while the latter’s likelihood provides a reference for preventing likelihood inflation, since increases beyond the unconstrained reference need not reflect better answers. These likelihoods define the region’s lower and upper bounds, respectively. We retain the verifier reward below the lower bound, add a fixed bonus within the region when the verifier reward is positive, and set the total reward to zero above the upper bound. In practice, CaLIF adds little overhead: it reuses the reference policy already maintained for KL regularization, computes both bounds offline, and requires at most one extra teacher-forced forward pass per rollout. (a) Constraint Satisfaction vs. Response Quality . (b) Response Quality with and without constraint. Figure 1: An evaluation blind spot in VIF: evidence from frontier models on IFBench. Constraint Satisfaction evaluates whether responses satisfy the constraints using programmatic verifiers; Response Quality evaluates how well they answer the request using three LLM judges: GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, whose scores are averaged. Pink arrows show the drop in Response Quality from answering the request alone to answering the request with added constraints. Across five model configurations spanning 1.7B to 8B parameters and including both thinking and non-thinking modes, CaLIF improves Constraint Satisfaction on IFBench while keeping Response Quality near or above base-policy levels. On average across these configurations, IF-RLVR increases Constraint Satisfaction (0–100 scale) from 26.98 to 44.93 but reduces Response Quality (1–10 scale) from 4.51 to 2.96, while CaLIF improves both metrics to 34.64 and 4.59, respectively. Focusing on prompts where the base policy fails constraint verification but the trained policy passes, we find an average decline in Response Quality of 0.28 points under CaLIF , compared with 2.05 under IF-RLVR, which indicates that CaLIF learns to satisfy constraints with substantially less degradation in its answers to the request. Importantly, these gains generalize to three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, where CaLIF outperforms baselines in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons, versus only 14 of 45 for IF-RLVR. These results demonstrate that CaLIF ’s reference-calibrated reward provides an effective signal for mitigating reward hacking in IF-RLVR without any additional models or explicit supervision. CaLIF thus brings the scalability of verifiable rewards to the full objective of instruction following: satisfying constraints while adequately answering the request. The model achieves a high Response Quality score of 9.33 when given the request alone, but its constrained response includes exactly five numbers as required while scoring only 2.00 in Response Quality . 2 Related Work 2.1 Instruction-Following Evaluation Instruction following has been extensively studied as a core capability of LLMs. MT-Bench ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) and AlpacaEval ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) use LLM judges to rate response quality or compare responses, providing a scalable alternative to human evaluation. Further work extends LLM-based evaluation to individual requirements and their combinations, using task-specific rubrics for finer-grained assessment ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks assess satisfaction of explicit constraints through programmatic checks rather than LLM judgments, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation ( He et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Jaroslawicz et al., 2025 ; Liquid AI, 2026 ) . As an example, IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) covers constraints on response length, keyword inclusion, and output format, while IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) extends this approach to a broader range of output constraints. 2.2 Reward Hacking in RLVR Reward hacking occurs when optimizing a proxy reward leads to behavior that diverges from the intended objective ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Pan et al., 2022 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ) . In RLVR, models can exploit flaws or misspecifications in verification procedures to obtain higher rewards without improving performance on the intended task ( Baker et al., 2025 ; MacDiarmid et al., 2025 ; Helff et al., 2026 ) , with related concerns reported in IF-RLVR ( Guo et al., 2025b ; Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) . To mitigate this behavior, prior work supplements verifiable rewards with explicit feedback on instruction fulfillment, using learned preference reward models ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) or LLM-based intent checks ( Guo et al., 2025b ) . These approaches, however, require maintaining and querying an additional reward model or LLM judge during training, introducing memory and inference overhead. 3 The Evaluation Blind Spot in Verifiable Instruction Following Instruction-following benchmarks assess how well a model’s response y y fulfills the user’s request and requirements. Because evaluating open-ended responses relies on costly human assessment or potentially biased LLM judgments ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) , verifiable instruction-following (VIF) benchmarks such as IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) focus on programmatically verifiable requirements. Specifically, these benchmarks append output constraints c c to a request x x and use programmatic verifiers to check whether y y satisfies c c , enabling scalable, reproducible evaluation without relying on LLM judges. Successful instruction following requires y y to satisfy c c while providing a substantive answer to x x , but standard VIF evaluation focuses primarily on constraint compliance. In practice, Artificial Analysis and several frontier model technical reports use only IFBench’s constraint compliance scores to assess models’ instruction-following performance ( Artificial Analysis, 2026 ) . To examine how frontier models balance these requirements, we evaluate both Constraint Satisfaction , which measures whether y y satisfies c c , and Response Quality , which measures how well y y answers x x . We compute the former as IFBench’s prompt-level loose accuracy and the latter as the mean 1–10 prompt–completion rating from strong LLM judges (see Appendix A for details). Figure 1(a) shows substantial variation across models, with higher Constraint Satisfaction tending to coincide with lower Response Quality . To assess whether this relationship simply reflects differences in models’ ability to answer x x , we compare each model’s responses under x x and ( x , c ) (x,c) . Figure 1(b) shows that all models in this comparison achieve high Response Quality under x x alone, but appending c c degrades Response Quality , with the largest declines among models with the highest Constraint Satisfaction . Figure 2 illustrates this degradation in a model that provides a substantive explanation under x x alone but returns only “No. 0 1 2 3 4,” under ( x , c ) (x,c) . Standard VIF evaluation counts this response as successful solely because it satisfies c c , exposing an evaluation blind spot . Figure 3: Comparison of DPO and RLVR checkpoints in the OLMo 3 family on IFBench. Log-likelihood is computed under the corresponding DPO checkpoint, conditioned on the request alone. IF-RLVR ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Pyatkin et al., 2025 ) extends this verifier-based criterion from evaluation to training, applying RLVR to instruction following with rewards derived from programmatic verification of the appended constraints. However, models trained with RL for instruction following ( NVIDIA, 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) tend to show high Constraint Satisfaction but low Response Quality , as noted above. Furthermore, in all three matched OLMo 3 ( Olmo et al., 2025 ) DPO–RLVR pairs, the RLVR checkpoint achieves higher Constraint Satisfaction but lower Response Quality (Figure 3 ). These observations are consistent with reward hacking under IF-RLVR, where models improve verifier rewards at the expense of response quality ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Pan et al., 2022 ) . 4 CaLIF : Calibrated Likelihood for Instruction Following Given a VIF instance ( x , c ) (x,c) with c = ( c 1 , … , c n ) c=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}) , our goal is to obtain a response y y that maximizes its probability under a target distribution p ⁡ ( y ∣ x , c ) p(y\mid x,c) . We train Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B in both thinking and non-thinking modes ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and Tülu 3 8B DPO ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) in verl . 2 2 2 https://github.com/verl-project/verl We use matched training settings for CaLIF and IF-RLVR, with a rollout temperature of 1.0 1.0 and a KL loss coefficient β = 0.001 \beta=0.001 , and set likelihood reward coefficient α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 for CaLIF . For offline reference generation, responses are sampled with a temperature of 1.0 1.0 . In thinking mode, responses include reasoning traces, but only final answers are scored under the reference policy in non-thinking mode. For evaluation, we follow the providers’ recommended settings and report the mean and standard deviation over three runs. request alone as a term omitted by IF-RLVR’s verifier reward. To test whether directly rewarding this term preserves Response Quality , we exponentiate the average token log-likelihood to obtain a positive reward bounded by the same α \alpha used in CaLIF . The bonus is applied only when a response receives a positive verifier reward: r direct ( x , c , y ) = r ver ( c , y ) + α exp ( ℓ π ref ( y ; x ) ) [ r ver ( c , y ) > 0 ] . r_{\mathrm{direct}}(x,c,y)=r_{\mathrm{ver}}(c,y)+\alpha\exp\!\left(\ell_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y;x)\right)\mathbf{1}\!\left[r_{\mathrm{ver}}(c,y)>0\right]. However, we find that training with this reward introduces another shortcut (i.e., likelihood inflation ). Relative to the base policy, average reference log-likelihood rises from − 1.50 -1.50 to − 0.68 -0.68 , while Response Quality falls from 3.98 3.98 to 1.91 1.91 (Table 4 ). This deterioration is accompanied by longer, repetitive responses: the average response length increases from 485 to 1,677 tokens, and the fraction of unique token 2-grams is 0.177 0.177 , compared with 0.713 0.713 for the base policy and 0.698 0.698 for CaLIF . The direct reward favors these highly predictable continuations even when they provide less substantive answers to the request, thereby creating another risk to increase reward without improving response quality. We present a qualitative example of likelihood inflation in Appendix D.3 . 6.2 Both Likelihood Bounds Are Necessary Table 4 shows that the lower and upper likelihood bounds address distinct failure modes. Without the lower bound, low-likelihood responses remain eligible for the bonus: Constraint Satisfaction rises to 43.00 43.00 , but Response Quality falls to 2.16 2.16 . Without the upper bound, responses above the desired region remain eligible for the bonus, leaving the reward vulnerable to likelihood inflation; Response Quality falls to 3.51 3.51 despite increased reference log-likelihood. Among these variants, only the full region improves both dimensions over the base policy. The lower bound discourages deterioration relative to the pre-RL baseline, while the upper bound limits exploitation of the likelihood signal. 6.3 Robustness to Likelihood Bound Estimation Because the likelihood bounds are derived from stochastic offline rollouts, we test sensitivity to the sampled reference responses. We use the inward endpoints to construct a narrower likelihood region and the outward endpoints to construct a wider one. Appendix C Rubric-Based Instruction-Following Benchmarks AdvancedIF. AdvancedIF ( He et al., 2026 ) evaluates instruction following using expert-written rubrics across three categories: ComplexIF (CIF), Carried Context (CC), and System Steerability (SS). In our experiments, we evaluate only CIF, which focuses on single-turn requests with multiple requirements. We report Overall Pass Rate , the percentage of responses satisfying all rubric criteria, and Micro Rubric Pass Rate , the percentage of satisfied criteria pooled across responses. FollowBench. FollowBench ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) covers Content, Situation, Style, Format, and Example constraints, along with their combinations (Mixed), across five difficulty levels that progressively add constraints. We report Hard Satisfaction Rate (HSR), the percentage of responses satisfying all constraints; Soft Satisfaction Rate (SSR), the average fraction of constraints satisfied; and Consistent Satisfaction Levels (CSL), the average number of consecutive levels fully satisfied. ComplexBench. ComplexBench ( Wen et al., 2024 ) evaluates instructions combining constraints through conjunctions, conditional branches, and sequential dependencies. We report scoring-question accuracy for Lexical , Semantic , Utility , and Format constraints, covering word usage, semantic requirements, answer usefulness and factuality, and output format and length, respectively.
